result:
I keep thinking about the word *glass* and how it does something impossible in English. I say it out loud and I get a flash of cold, of the way it catches light at an angle, of the way my mother's fingers traced the rim of a wine glass while she was still alive, of a pane fogged up on a November morning, of a screen cracked in two across a kitchen table. You say *glass* and maybe you get only the material. Maybe you get a science fact. Maybe you get absolutely nothing, just a two-syllable sound passing through the room.

But here's the thing that never stops being strange to me: the word doesn't carry those things. The words are the same words. The same little phonemes. And yet every person who has ever spoken the word carries inside their skull a different mosaic of memories, textures, temperatures, and failures of memory. We pass them to each other like tokens, assuming the coin has a fixed value on the other side of the table.

I think this is why novels matter. Not because they describe well, but because they are attempts to build a bridge between the specific mosaic of one person's *glass* and the specific mosaic of another's. Not perfectly. Never perfectly. But close enough that when you finish the book, you have slightly more colors in the pane of glass in your own head than before.

And if that's not worth a little attention, I don't know what is.
